purpose: Hit the ball over the net with a balanced, body-driven swing: turn early, rotate the hips and shoulders through the ball, keep the hitting arm extending away from the body, and finish with a full follow-through. The result is controlled pace and direction into the target area.

phases.description: From the ready or recovered position the hitting arm lifts away from the trunk, the racket is prepared and swung forward; the phase ends at the point of greatest arm lift and spread (shoulder angle about 64 degrees, wrists furthest apart), which is the contact and early follow-through zone.
The arm wraps through the finish and comes back down toward the body as the player recovers to the ready position, with the wrists coming back together.

outcomes.description: The ball goes over the net with the intended pace, depth and direction.
The ball is struck cleanly in front of the body, at a good distance from it, with the arm extended.
The swing is balanced, rotates the body and finishes fully; the form alone is the point.

links.mechanism: Torso rotation passes the legs' and hips' energy to the arm, so too little loses power and too much loses control of the racket face.
An arm extended to a comfortable distance puts contact out in front of the body, while a cramped or overstretched arm mistimes the strike.
Body weight moving neutrally to forward keeps the ball in front of the body and the strike on time.

objectives.goal: Rotate the hips and shoulders through the shot so the shoulder line has turned with the swing at contact.

below.looks_like: Torso stays square or blocked, the arm swings alone and the shoulders are behind at contact.

above.looks_like: Over-rotation, with the shoulders spun far ahead of the hips and the body pulling around too early.

objectives.cue_intent: Prompt the player to turn the body through the ball, not just swing the arm.
objectives.ask_if_unsure_intent: Ask whether the player feels the hips and chest turning, or whether the feet are stuck or blocking the rotation.
objectives.fix_intent: Give a drill that links the leg push and hip turn to the swing, such as shadow swings that finish with the belt buckle facing the target.

objectives.goal: Let the hitting arm extend away from the body and up through contact, not bend and pull in toward the body.

below.looks_like: The elbow collapses and the hand cuts down and in toward the body, so contact is cramped.

above.looks_like: Arm fully stretched out, reaching for a ball that is too far away.

objectives.cue_intent: Prompt the player to extend the hitting arm out and through the ball.
objectives.ask_if_unsure_intent: Ask whether the ball felt too close to the body at contact.
objectives.fix_intent: Give a drill that adjusts spacing and has the player hit out in front with room between the arm and the body.

objectives.goal: Swing through the ball into a complete, unhurried finish instead of stopping the arm early.

below.looks_like: The arm stops or bends low and the finish is short or rushed. Coaches disagree whether the finish should be over the shoulder or across the body, so only a stopped finish counts as the fault.

objectives.cue_intent: Prompt the player to keep the racket moving through to a full finish.
objectives.ask_if_unsure_intent: Ask whether the player is holding back out of fear of hitting long.
objectives.fix_intent: Give a finish-and-hold drill at slow pace, then add pace while keeping the same finish.

objectives.goal: Set up with the body at a comfortable distance from the ball, with weight moving neutrally or forward through contact.

below.looks_like: Weight stays back or travels backward and the ball ends up behind the body.

above.looks_like: Crowding the ball, or leaning forward and jamming the arm.

objectives.cue_intent: Prompt the player to adjust their footwork to get the right distance from the ball.
objectives.ask_if_unsure_intent: Ask whether the ball feels too close or too far at contact, or whether the player is being pushed back.
objectives.fix_intent: Give a footwork drill using small adjustment steps, with feeds that vary in depth.

objectives.goal: Use the non-hitting arm to help balance and turn, extended in the preparation and then drawn in smoothly, not left dangling or flung away.

below.looks_like: The free arm hangs or hugs the body, so balance and rotation are poor.

above.looks_like: The free arm splits away early or flails outward, which pulls the shoulders off line.

objectives.cue_intent: Prompt the player to keep the free hand out in front for balance, then tuck it in during the swing.
objectives.ask_if_unsure_intent: Ask what the free hand is doing during the swing.
objectives.fix_intent: Give a drill where the free hand points at or touches the racket in the preparation.

session_ideas: Shadow swings in slow motion, with a hold at the finish
Drop-feed forehands to a target, with the focus on rotation
Footwork drill that adds adjustment steps before each ball
Cross-court rally with the aim of finishing every swing fully

good_form.point: Accelerate as a kinetic chain from the ground up: legs, hips, trunk, then arm.
Stay balanced with weight moving forward or neutral, and keep enough space from the ball.
Take the racket back by turning the whole body, with the racket going along.
Start the take-back early, as soon as you read the ball, without waiting for the bounce.
Use the non-hitting hand to help the racket back, stay coiled, and catch the racket at the finish.
Make contact out in front of the body with the arm in front and the wrist extended.
Keep the wrist and grip loose and passive through contact, and don't tense.
Finish with a smooth, continuous, full follow-through and never stop the racket.
Let the racket drop fluidly on the hitting side and keep it moving without stopping.
At the end of the backswing the tip is up with the strings angled down, so the face is closed.
Rotation is a main power source, and the dominant shoulder should be in front at contact.
Use a compact take-back with a long follow-through for timing and control.
Match footwork to the ball so you can rotate: set the feet, or hit off the back foot when pushed back.
In the unit turn the right elbow is bent about 90 degrees, or roughly in line with the shoulders.
Load the hips and release them like a slingshot so the upper body keeps rotating.
Swing up an incline with the racket face tilted slightly forward to create topspin.
Pull the arm away from the body in acceleration to create the racket flip.
Aim at a specific target and play crosscourt in rally and defense.
Bent-arm and straight-arm forehands both work.
Check the grip so the contact angle is right.

faults.description: Late racket and foot preparation or mistimed swing, including waiting for the bounce.

causes.cause: Waiting for the bounce before taking the racket back
Misreading the ball's height, speed, depth or spin
Ready position that doesn't suit the forehand, or no split step
Trying advanced pro technique beyond current skill
Slow footwork habits

fixes.idea: Begin the take-back as soon as the ball leaves the opponent's racket.
Work one feed at a time on a ball machine, a few hundred reps each.
Time hip drive to the bounce.
Simplify to unit turn, racket set, then swing through.
Hold the racket mostly horizontal in the ready position with the off hand on the neck.

outcome_effects: Late contact, not out in front
Trouble with fast or deep balls

faults.description: The finish is short, rushed, too low, or the arm stops and bends across the body.

causes.cause: Not finishing all the way through or finishing too quickly
Catching the ball late and stopping to control it

fixes.idea: Make the motion smooth and continuous, finishing over the shoulder.
Keep the arm extending forward and out through the ball.
Finish around the tricep, deltoid or over the trap.

outcome_effects: A lower finish sends the ball lower
faults.disagreement: Source 11 finishes over the shoulder. Source 8 finishes across the body, and source 1 says follow-throughs vary on tour.

faults.description: The racket is taken back by the arm alone with no body turn.

causes.cause: Hitting with the dominant arm instead of turning the whole body
Trying to hit hard

fixes.idea: Rotate the core smoothly so the body takes the racket back.
Self feeds: hold a ball in the spare hand, turn sideways, drop and hit.
Hit a double-handed forehand to force the upper-body turn.

outcome_effects: Tension in the arm and extra arm workload, which can lead to injury
Less power from the body turn

faults.description: The arm is too straight in the unit turn, or a bent-arm player forces a straight arm.

causes.cause: Taking the racket back with too much arm energy
Copying the straight-arm style of Nadal and Federer

fixes.idea: Check the elbow is bent about 90 degrees, or in line with the shoulders, in the unit turn.
Film your stroke and compare it with top players.

outcome_effects: Forehand feels tight, rushed or late
Extra unnecessary motion in the backswing
faults.disagreement: Sources 0 and 1 want a bent or in-line elbow in the unit turn. Source 8 says bent or straight doesn't matter, so don't force a straight arm.
faults.note: angle.elbow.dom shows arm straightness; no test because the right value depends on player style.

faults.description: The racket face angle at contact is wrong: vertical, too closed, or turned toward the body.

causes.cause: Thinking only of down-to-up and ignoring the forward plane
Brushing up with a closed angle when lacking strength
Imagining hitting up a vertical wall

fixes.idea: Keep a slightly forward-tilted face and imagine swinging up a steep slope.
Use an open contact angle if weak, adjusting it with the shoulder.
Keep the palm and racquet face pointing away from the body through the finish.
Shadow strokes and ball-on-racket-bag incline drill.

outcome_effects: Shanks and balls into the net
faults.disagreement: Source 4 says tilt the face forward, and source 9 says beginners should use an open angle.
faults.note: racket detection (racket face orientation) or hand landmarks for forearm rotation

faults.description: The non-hitting hand dangles, splits away early, or hugs the body.

causes.cause: Pulling the off hand away or opening the chest before contact
Pointing at the ball and then hugging yourself
Letting the off arm hang at the side

fixes.idea: Stay coiled and drive the off-hand elbow back, tucking it to the chest as the hips move.
Turn with both hands and catch the racket at the finish for a second.
Catch-drop-hit with the spare hand.
Imagine handcuffs: keep the hands together until the ball bounces.

outcome_effects: Ball sprays or is dragged across
Hips can't turn and the racket can't come through freely
The hitting arm works harder, which can lead to injuries

faults.description: Standing too close or too far from the ball, including stepping into a closed stance on every ball.

causes.cause: Stepping into closed stance on every ball
Poor spacing habits and late reading
Lack of practiced footwork patterns

fixes.idea: Stay in open stance and use swing and gallop to fix the distance.
Practice staying farther from the ball on each feed type.
One-legged tennis to feel when you are too close or far.
Practice footwork patterns off court.

outcome_effects: Cramped arm, wrist bending or snatching
faults.disagreement: Source 9 says stay open and don't step into every ball. Sources 7 and 10 say step in for neutral stance and step into the ball.

faults.description: Rotation is late, too large, or blocked by footwork or stance, so the shoulder is behind at contact.

causes.cause: Rotation not started before the racket goes forward
Turn too large, with the off hand past the middle of the body
Sideways momentum or planted feet locking the torso
Choosing a stance for the ball's position instead of balance and rotation
Contact at the end of the arm's range

fixes.idea: Start rotation slightly before the racket moves forward, around the racket drop.
Release the off hand at the middle of the body, using the lace line.
Hit off the non-dominant foot or set the outside foot to break momentum.
Turn the toe out when stepping forward.
Work on rotation, footwork and arm range before the swing.

outcome_effects: Contact with the dominant shoulder behind

faults.description: The take-back is too big, with a short follow-through, so contact is late.

causes.cause: Trying for power
Big swing against fast balls with little time
Not aware of the real swing size

fixes.idea: Shorten the backswing and lengthen the follow-through.
Video your forehand to see the real take-back size.
Stand sideways to a fence so a big take-back hits it.
Pair the short backswing with coiling and leg drive.

faults.disagreement: Source 11 says to take the racquet all the way back behind you while staying compact. Sources 2 and 3 push a smaller take-back.

faults.description: The arm lifts up and back, loops, or the racket drops twice on the way back.

causes.cause: Dropping the racket on the way back before the normal drop behind the body
Not trusting a simple fluid drop
Judging arm action by watching the racket instead of the arm

fixes.idea: Keep the racket up on the way back and let it drop once, behind you.
Swing in a C shape so the racket never stops.
Push the arm back with the body turn instead of looping it.

outcome_effects: Lost fluid momentum and racket flip position
The racket stops and struggles against hard hitters
faults.disagreement: Source 9 says don't loop the arm. Sources 5 and 6 recommend a loop or circle path for the racket.
faults.note: wrist trajectory path during backswing (wrist position over time relative to shoulder/trunk, loop detection)

faults.description: The arm bends or travels down and in toward the body instead of away and up.

causes.cause: Flexing the bicep and wrist to swing
Not having the proper backswing position

fixes.idea: Pull the arm away from the body, down-and-away or up-and-away.
Accelerate with shoulder flexion, horizontal adduction and external rotation.

faults.description: The swing is started and powered by the arm instead of the legs driving and rotating.

causes.cause: Not starting the swing from the ground up
Not focusing on footwork or leg force

fixes.idea: Drive with the legs first, then rotate the trunk, then let the arm move.
Use footwork such as the transfer move, lateral hop or front-foot hop.

faults.disagreement: Source 9 disagrees: legs are complementary and the arm leads.
faults.note: sequencing of leg extension (knee/hip angle change) before arm movement; timing/order of joint velocities

faults.description: The ball gets behind the body, or weight travels backward, when pushed back.

causes.cause: Standing too close to a heavy or deep ball
Not moving the feet fast enough
Poor reading of the ball's depth

fixes.idea: Stand farther back against big hitters so you can step in.
Widen the base against balls at the feet.
Keep the body behind the ball and hit off the back foot, letting the other foot swing back.

faults.disagreement: Source 3 says weight should go forward or stay neutral. Source 5 says keep the body behind the ball and hit off the back foot.

faults.description: Choosing the wrong shot for the phase of play or hitting with no target over the net.

causes.cause: Favoring the forehand tempts players into risky shots
No specific target chosen before the shot

fixes.idea: Stick to crosscourt in defense and rally, and save down the line for attack.
Pick an air target over the net on every shot, higher the farther back you are.

outcome_effects: Less control of depth and net clearance

faults.description: The racket is pre-flipped, open, or held straight up and down in the backswing, so the swing goes flat.

causes.cause: Arm travelling too far back with an open face
Racket held vertical instead of closed below contact

fixes.idea: Finish the backswing with the tip up at about 45 degrees and the strings angled down.
Close the face below contact and swing up the back of the ball.

outcome_effects: Racket not closed on acceleration, losing easy shoulder power
Can't dip the ball or hit topspin lobs
faults.note: racket detection or hand landmarks for racket face orientation

faults.description: The grip is too tight or the body tenses at contact.

causes.cause: Natural urge to tense at contact
Worn overgrip makes you grip hard

fixes.idea: Let go and let the racquet and rotation do the work.
Breathe out as you hit.
Replace the overgrip often.

outcome_effects: Swipe across the body with no topspin roll

faults.description: The wrist flexes at contact with the arm too close to the body or too bent.

causes.cause: Trying to generate power from the wrist
Arm too close to the trunk or abducted
Tight wrist

fixes.idea: Contact with the arm in front of the body, wrist extended, palm to the net.
Stop shadow swings at contact, then fed balls at contact, then build to full power.
Grip with only the index and middle fingers and shadow swing with a loose wrist.
Let the wrist make a windshield-wiper motion in the follow-through.

faults.description: Faking wrist lag or actively flicking the wrist at contact.

causes.cause: Consciously thinking about the wrist
Not realizing lag comes from torso rotation and acceleration

fixes.idea: Don't think about the wrist and let lag happen from rotation.
Think about finishing strongly across the body.

faults.disagreement: Source 1 wants an active windshield-wiper wrist, and source 0 wants a flip. Source 8 wants the wrist passive at contact.
faults.note: hand landmarks or racket tracking for wrist flick; intent is not visible

faults.description: Driving with the legs while the arm is still, or keeping the legs locked.

causes.cause: Belief that most power comes from the legs

fixes.idea: Let the arm lead and use squat, right lunge, then calf raise in sync with the swing.

faults.disagreement: Sources 0, 1 and 3 teach leg drive first as the power source.
faults.note: coordination of leg drive versus arm movement over time (knee/hip extension timing relative to arm swing)

faults.description: The grip is rotated wrongly in the hand or the wrong size.

causes.cause: Wrong rotation angle of the racket in the hand

fixes.idea: Put the middle and ring fingertips on a short side followed by an open medium side.
Check the grip size fits the hand.

outcome_effects: Contact angle is wrong and the ball is missed
faults.note: hand landmarks for grip rotation in the hand; racket detection for grip size

principles.statement: Power builds from the ground up: legs and hips turn first, then the trunk, then the arm and racket. The arm adds speed at the end of the chain instead of creating it, so the shoulder line has turned with the swing by contact.
alternatives: Sources 0, 1 and 3 teach leg drive first as the main power source.
Source 9 says the legs are complementary and the arm leads the swing.

principles.statement: A comfortable distance from the ball leaves room for the arm to extend away from the body and up through contact. If the ball is too close or the arm bends in, the lever is cramped and the swing loses reach and speed.
principles.handle_intent: Keep room to reach out and up through the ball.
alternatives: Sources 7 and 10 say to step in with a neutral stance and step into the ball.
Source 9 says to stay open and not step into every ball.
Source 3 says weight should go forward or stay neutral when pushed back; Source 5 says to hit off the back foot, body behind the ball.

principles.statement: Getting the turn and racket ready early gives time to set up and swing at an even pace. Late preparation forces a rushed or mistimed swing. A compact preparation keeps contact on time.
principles.handle_intent: Be set and ready before the ball arrives so the swing flows at an even rhythm.
alternatives: Source 11 says to take the racquet all the way back while staying compact; Sources 2 and 3 push a smaller take-back.
Sources 5 and 6 recommend a looped racket path; Source 9 says not to loop the arm.
Sources 0 and 1 want a bent or in-line elbow in the unit turn; Source 8 says bent or straight does not matter.

principles.statement: Keep the racket moving through the ball into a full, unhurried finish. The arm then keeps accelerating through contact instead of braking early, and the speed bleeds off smoothly on the way to recovery.
principles.handle_intent: Keep accelerating through the ball and let the swing finish on its own.
alternatives: Source 1 says follow-throughs vary on tour.

principles.statement: The non-hitting arm acts as a counterweight. Extended during preparation, it helps balance and turn the trunk, then it draws in smoothly so the body stays stable and the turn is controlled. Dangling or flinging it away upsets balance.
principles.handle_intent: Stay balanced and turn smoothly, with both sides working together.
